cards.q: Why can two processes not share data by writing to the same address?
cards.a: Each has its own private address space; the same address refers to different memory in each.

cards.q: Why is holding a process handle better than remembering its PID?
cards.a: The PID can be reused by another process once the original ends; a handle keeps referring to the same process object.

cards.q: Name four ways processes on one machine can exchange data or signals.
cards.a: Any four of: pipes, file mappings (shared memory), sockets, named events, mutexes and semaphores, window messages, files.

cards.q: What happens to a pipe when the process at its other end crashes?
cards.a: Windows closes that process's handles, so the pipe is closed and the next read or write fails.

cards.q: How does an environment block end?
cards.a: Each NAME=value string ends with a zero, and the whole block ends with one more zero.

cards.q: In what order must variables appear in an environment block?
cards.a: Sorted by name, ignoring case.

cards.q: What goes wrong when inheritHandles is TRUE without a handle list in a multi-threaded program?
cards.a: The child inherits every inheritable handle, including ones other threads just created, which can keep pipes and files open unexpectedly.

cards.q: Why start a child with CREATE_SUSPENDED?
cards.a: To do something before it runs any code, such as adding it to a job object.

cards.q: Why should a wait for a child process always have a timeout?
cards.a: A hung child would otherwise freeze the parent indefinitely.

cards.q: A helper's exit code is 0xC0000005. What happened?
cards.a: It crashed with an access violation; Windows ended it after the unhandled exception.

cards.q: Why is TerminateProcess a last resort?
cards.a: It ends the process immediately with no clean-up: no destructors, no flushing, possibly corrupt files.

cards.q: What does JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE give you?
cards.a: Every process in the job is ended when the last job handle closes, even if the parent crashes.

cards.q: Why must the parent close its copy of the child's stdout write handle after starting it?
cards.a: End-of-file is reported only when every write handle is closed; otherwise reading never finishes.

cards.q: Describe the stdout and stderr deadlock.
cards.a: The parent reads stdout to the end while the child blocks writing to a full stderr pipe; each waits for the other.

cards.q: Why can a single read return half a line?
cards.a: Pipes carry bytes in arbitrary chunks; line boundaries are not preserved.

cards.q: How does the Language Server Protocol mark where a message ends?
cards.a: A Content-Length header gives the body's size, followed by a blank line and exactly that many bytes.

cards.q: Which method has no per-byte cost once set up, and what does it lack?
cards.a: Shared memory; it has no built-in framing or synchronisation, so you build structures and signalling yourself.

cards.q: Which methods tell you automatically when the other side has died?
cards.a: Pipes and sockets: the connection is closed and reads or writes fail.

cards.q: Two unrelated programs need to talk. What do they need that a parent and child do not?
cards.a: A name both know: a pipe name, a mapping name or a port number.

cards.q: Why might you choose sockets even when both processes are on one machine?
cards.a: The same protocol and code then work across a network, and every language supports them.

cards.q: Two writes of 4 bytes each go into a pipe. What might a single read of 16 bytes return?
cards.a: Anything from the first few bytes up to all 8: a pipe keeps no message boundaries.

cards.q: How does a reader of an anonymous pipe recognise end-of-file?
cards.a: ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE once every write handle is closed and the buffer is empty.

cards.q: Why can't an unrelated program connect to an anonymous pipe?
cards.a: It has no name; a process can only use it if given a handle by inheritance or duplication.

cards.q: How do you check whether data is waiting without blocking?
cards.a: PeekNamedPipe reports the number of bytes available.

cards.q: What does one call to CreateNamedPipeW create?
cards.a: One instance: a single connection slot that one client at a time can use.

cards.q: A client gets ERROR_PIPE_BUSY. What does it mean and what should it do?
cards.a: The server exists but every instance is in use; call WaitNamedPipeW and try to connect again.

cards.q: In message mode, what does ERROR_MORE_DATA on a read mean?
cards.a: The message is longer than the buffer; the bytes so far were returned and more of the same message follows.

cards.q: Are pipe names case-sensitive?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: Why is a newline delimiter a poor choice for binary messages?
cards.a: The newline byte can appear inside binary data, so the reader would split a message in the wrong place unless everything is escaped.

cards.q: A frame header says the payload is 3 000 000 000 bytes. What should the reader do?
cards.a: Treat it as a protocol error, refuse to allocate, and close the connection.

cards.q: Why close the connection after a framing error rather than skip the bad message?
cards.a: After a bad length the reader no longer knows where the next frame starts, so nothing after it can be trusted.

cards.q: What must a message-mode reader do when a read fails with ERROR_MORE_DATA?
cards.a: Keep the bytes and read again to get the rest of the same message, joining the pieces.

cards.q: How does a pipe server handle three clients at the same time?
cards.a: It creates three instances of the same pipe name, one per connection, usually one new instance per accept-loop iteration.

cards.q: Why might a client get ERROR_PIPE_BUSY even though the server serves unlimited clients?
cards.a: Between one connection being accepted and the next instance being created, there is briefly no free instance.

cards.q: When is a thread per client a poor choice?
cards.a: With hundreds or thousands of clients, where threads' memory and scheduling costs grow too large.

cards.q: Why is the client's PID not proof of its identity?
cards.a: PIDs are reused and any process can connect; only the pipe's access control decides who may connect.

cards.q: What must stay alive until an overlapped operation completes?
cards.a: The OVERLAPPED structure and the buffer passed to the call.

cards.q: What does ERROR_IO_PENDING from ReadFile on an overlapped handle mean?
cards.a: The read has started and will complete later; it is not a failure.

cards.q: What does the key passed to CreateIoCompletionPort give a worker thread?
cards.a: A value identifying the handle's connection, usually a pointer to its state, returned with every completion.

cards.q: Why do servers using completion ports structure connections as state machines?
cards.a: Each completion arrives separately on whichever worker is free, so each connection must remember what it is waiting for and start the next operation itself.

cards.q: Why is shared memory faster than a pipe for large amounts of data?
cards.a: Nothing is copied: both processes see the same physical pages.

cards.q: Why is a pointer stored in shared memory useless to the other process?
cards.a: The view is mapped at different addresses in each process.

cards.q: What is the difference between Local\name and Global\name?
cards.a: Local is visible only within the current session; Global is visible across sessions and needs a privilege to create.

cards.q: When does a page-file backed mapping's content disappear?
cards.a: When the last handle is closed and the last view is unmapped in every process.

cards.q: Why store offsets instead of pointers in shared memory?
cards.a: Each process maps the block at a different address; an offset from the block's start means the same in all of them.

cards.q: Why is std::string unsuitable as a member of a shared struct?
cards.a: It owns heap memory in its own process; the other process would see a pointer into a heap it cannot access.

cards.q: What are a shared header's magic number, version and size for?
cards.a: To confirm the block is the right one, that its layout is understood, and to bound every offset read from it.

cards.q: Why must std::atomic be lock-free to work in shared memory?
cards.a: A lock-based atomic uses a lock in each process's own runtime that the other process cannot see.

cards.q: Why does an SPSC ring buffer need no lock?
cards.a: Each counter is written by only one side: the producer writes head, the consumer writes tail.

cards.q: With ever-increasing counters, how do you test for full?
cards.a: head - tail == capacity.

cards.q: Why must the producer store the new head with release ordering after writing the slot?
cards.a: So that a consumer that sees the new head with an acquire load also sees the slot's contents.

cards.q: Why are ring capacities usually powers of two?
cards.a: The slot index becomes counter & (capacity - 1), avoiding a division, and counter wrap-around stays consistent.

cards.q: Why is mapping a 2 GB file and reading a few bytes from its end fast?
cards.a: Pages are read only when touched, so only the pages actually read are loaded.

cards.q: You want a view starting at file offset 200 000. Where must the view actually start?
cards.a: At 196 608 (3 × 65 536), the allocation granularity boundary below it; the data begins 3 392 bytes into the view.

cards.q: How do you make sure written data has reached the disk?
cards.a: FlushViewOfFile to write the changed pages, then FlushFileBuffers on the file handle.

cards.q: How does a disk error show up when reading through a mapped file?
cards.a: As an EXCEPTION_IN_PAGE_ERROR structured exception at the memory access.

cards.q: What is a torn read?
cards.a: A read that sees part of an old state and part of a new one, a combination that never existed.

cards.q: What does an odd sequence counter tell a seqlock reader?
cards.a: A write is in progress, so it must try again.

cards.q: Why does the reader read the counter a second time after copying?
cards.a: If it changed, a write happened during the copy and the copy may be torn.

cards.q: Why is a seqlock better than a mutex for a game publishing state to a tool?
cards.a: The writer never waits for readers, so a slow or stalled tool cannot slow the game.

cards.q: Two programs both call CreateEventW with the same name. What happens to the second call?
cards.a: It opens the existing event, succeeds, and GetLastError returns ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS; its initial-state arguments are ignored.

cards.q: When should a program use OpenEventW instead of CreateEventW?
cards.a: When it must not create the object itself, for example a client that should fail if the server is not running.

cards.q: When is a mutex signalled?
cards.a: When no thread owns it.

cards.q: When does a named kernel object disappear?
cards.a: When the last handle to it, in any process, is closed.

cards.q: When should an event be manual-reset rather than auto-reset?
cards.a: When it represents a state everyone should see, such as shutting down, and should stay set for all waiters.

cards.q: SetEvent is called three times on an auto-reset event before the consumer wakes. How many times does the consumer's wait succeed?
cards.a: Once: an event is a flag, not a counter. The consumer must drain all waiting work each time it wakes.

cards.q: How can a consumer of shared memory find out that the producer process has died?
cards.a: Include the producer's process handle in WaitForMultipleObjects; it becomes signalled when the process ends.

cards.q: With bWaitAll FALSE, which index is returned if two handles are signalled at once?
cards.a: The lowest one, so the most important handle should come first.

cards.q: What does WAIT_ABANDONED mean on a mutex wait?
cards.a: The caller now owns the mutex, but its previous owner ended while holding it, so the protected data may be inconsistent.

cards.q: Why is a Win32 mutex called recursive?
cards.a: The owning thread can wait on it again without blocking, releasing it once per successful wait.

cards.q: Why is there no abandonment for semaphores?
cards.a: A semaphore has no owner; any thread may release it, so Windows cannot know who should have.

cards.q: A semaphore created with initial count 4 and maximum 4 has five waiters. How many get through at once?
cards.a: Four; the fifth waits until one releases.

cards.q: Why can a normal message not carry a pointer to data for another process?
cards.a: The pointer refers to the sender's address space; the receiver cannot use it.

cards.q: How long is the data of a WM_COPYDATA message valid in the receiver?
cards.a: Only while the receiver is handling the message; it must copy what it needs before returning.

cards.q: Why use SendMessageTimeoutW rather than SendMessageW to another program?
cards.a: A hung receiver would otherwise hang the sender indefinitely.

cards.q: Why might WM_COPYDATA from a normal program never reach a program running as administrator?
cards.a: UIPI blocks messages to higher-integrity processes unless they explicitly allow that message.

cards.q: What shape does a deadlock have in a wait-for graph?
cards.a: A cycle: each participant waits for the next, and the last waits for the first.

cards.q: How does a global lock order prevent lock-order deadlocks?
cards.a: Every process takes locks in increasing rank, so no cycle of waiting can form.

cards.q: Why should a lock never be held during a pipe write or SendMessage?
cards.a: If the peer is slow, hung or waiting for that same lock, the holder blocks everyone waiting for the lock too.

cards.q: An event the other process should set never arrives. Why should the wait have a timeout?
cards.a: The other process may have died; a timeout lets you check whether it is alive instead of waiting for ever.

cards.q: Why bind a local IPC server to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0?
cards.a: 0.0.0.0 accepts connections from the network and triggers a firewall prompt; 127.0.0.1 accepts only local processes.

cards.q: Why bind to port 0?
cards.a: The system chooses a free port, avoiding collisions with other programs and other copies of your own.

cards.q: How does a client find a server that bound to port 0?
cards.a: The server writes the chosen port (with its PID and a token) to a file the client knows to read.

cards.q: What controls who may connect to an AF_UNIX socket?
cards.a: The permissions of its path in the file system.

cards.q: What is the magic number in a handshake for?
cards.a: To recognise immediately that the other side speaks this protocol at all, before parsing its bytes as messages.

cards.q: A client speaks 2.3 and the server 2.1. Which version do they use?
cards.a: 2.1: the same major version and the lower minor version.

cards.q: Why do all messages share one envelope?
cards.a: So any message can be framed, routed, matched and logged without understanding its specific payload.

cards.q: What should a receiver do with a request type it does not know?
cards.a: Reply with a "not supported" error and carry on, rather than crashing or closing the connection.

cards.q: Why not send a struct's raw bytes?
cards.a: Padding, type sizes, pointers to the sender's heap and layout changes between versions make the bytes mean different things to the receiver.

cards.q: Encode 300 as a varint.
cards.a: AC 02.

cards.q: Why zigzag-encode signed numbers before writing them as varints?
cards.a: Negative numbers would otherwise use the maximum number of bytes; zigzag maps small negatives to small positives.

cards.q: How does tag-length-value let old readers handle new fields?
cards.a: They skip any tag they do not know by its length and continue with the next field.

cards.q: How does a client match a response to its request?
cards.a: By the id it put in the request, which the response carries back.

cards.q: What should a client do with a response whose id matches no pending request?
cards.a: Log it and drop it; it is probably a late answer to a request that already timed out.

cards.q: Does one connection guarantee responses arrive in the order requests were sent?
cards.a: No: a concurrent server may finish requests in any order. Only messages in one direction are delivered in sending order.

cards.q: Which of these is safe to retry blindly: setVolume(70) or appendLog("x")?
cards.a: setVolume(70): it is idempotent. Repeating appendLog would add the line twice.

cards.q: What does FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE protect against?
cards.a: Pipe squatting: if another process already created the name, the server's creation fails instead of silently sharing it.

cards.q: Why do localhost TCP servers need a token?
cards.a: Any local process, and web pages via the browser, can connect to a localhost port; the token proves the client could read the user's private token file.

cards.q: How does checking the Host header defend against DNS rebinding?
cards.a: A rebinding request carries the attacker's domain name in Host; accepting only localhost:PORT rejects it.

cards.q: Why should a client open an untrusted pipe with SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION?
cards.a: So the server can identify the client but cannot impersonate it and act with its rights.

cards.q: How does a launched copy know another instance is already running?
cards.a: CreateMutexW on the shared name succeeds with ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS.

cards.q: Why must the secondary send its current directory with the arguments?
cards.a: Relative paths are relative to the secondary's folder, which the primary does not know.

cards.q: Why call AllowSetForegroundWindow in the secondary?
cards.a: Windows only lets the process the user just launched take the foreground; this passes that right to the primary.

cards.q: Why should the secondary retry forwarding for a short time?
cards.a: The primary may have created the mutex but not yet its pipe or window when two copies start almost together.

cards.q: Name two reasons to run work in a separate process instead of a thread.
cards.a: Any two of: crash isolation, memory isolation, running with fewer rights, parallel work without shared state.

cards.q: Why use exponential backoff for restarts?
cards.a: A worker that fails immediately would otherwise restart in a tight loop; growing delays retry quickly at first and back off for persistent failures.

cards.q: When should a supervisor stop restarting a worker?
cards.a: When it has failed too many times within a period, such as 5 times in 10 minutes: a crash loop that needs a human.

cards.q: Why must the heartbeat come from the worker's main work loop?
cards.a: A separate timer thread could keep sending heartbeats while the real work is hung.

cards.q: What does running a plugin out of process protect the host from?
cards.a: The plugin's crashes, hangs and memory corruption; the host survives and can stop it at any time.

cards.q: Why read a manifest before starting a plugin?
cards.a: To check API compatibility, learn its events and commands, and start it lazily, all without running its code.

cards.q: A plugin times out on three commands in a minute. What should the host do?
cards.a: Disable it and tell the user which plugin was at fault.

cards.q: Why is a separate process alone not a security boundary against a malicious plugin?
cards.a: It still runs with the user's rights and can access the user's files directly; only a restricted token or sandbox prevents that.

cards.q: Why separate framing and protocol logic from the transport?
cards.a: So they can be tested with plain byte vectors, quickly and deterministically, without real processes or pipes.

cards.q: Name three faults a fault-injecting transport should simulate.
cards.a: Any three of: split and joined messages, delays and reordering, dropped connections, a killed peer, garbage input.

cards.q: Why normalise a transcript before comparing it with the golden one?
cards.a: Timestamps and generated ids change from run to run; normalising them leaves only differences that matter.

cards.q: Which tool shows the named pipes, events and mutexes a process has open?
cards.a: Process Explorer's handle view.

cards.q: Why does a browser move rendered frames through shared memory rather than pipes?
cards.a: They are large; shared memory avoids copying them, while small control messages go over pipes.

cards.q: What makes the Language Server Protocol usable from any editor and any language?
cards.a: It is a documented, language-neutral protocol (JSON-RPC over a simple transport), not a library API.

cards.q: Why can a service and a tray application not use a Local\ event to talk?
cards.a: They run in different sessions, and Local\ names are per session.

cards.q: Which of the seven design questions covers heartbeats and abandoned mutexes?
cards.a: What fails, and how do you notice.
